opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Tyrone, thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, and we don't work for any company, union or party. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Bet. Is this gonna take long? I'm good, just asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be like, it already took the tills, bro. The kiosks and the drive-through voice thing. So it's not just a search engine where I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'm on the fryer now, which is fine. My manager keeps writing me up for being late though, so that's more my problem than AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the job, try to show up on time. Mess around with AI for music beats and stuff. Maybe try a delivery app on my off days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kinda whatever. A little meh.

S0.say: It already took the tills: the kiosks and the drive-through voice ordering.
S0.think: He's on the fryer now; his lateness worries him more than AI.
S0.do: Tries to show up on time, makes beats with AI, and might try a delivery app on days off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's crazy they don't hire young people anymore. Where are we supposed to start?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer beginner jobs is bad for me. I'm a beginner at everything. Fast food was the job you get when you can't get anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hold onto this one, for real this time. Maybe look at that free coding thing online my cousin told me about. Probably won't finish it, not gonna lie.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you probably wouldn't finish the course. What would help you stick with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody making me. Like if it was a class with people, and they paid you to go. I don't do good on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Little stressed. Not like, crying about it.

S1.say: It's crazy they don't hire young people anymore. Where are we supposed to start?
S1.think: Fewer beginner jobs hurts him, since fast food is the job you get when nothing else works.
S1.do: Holds onto this job and might try a free online coding course, though he doubts he'd finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office people are gonna come take our jobs now. Watch, they'll be flipping burgers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's real. If people with degrees need work, they'll get hired over me. Managers like them more. I'd be the first one cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grind more on the delivery apps. Try to get a second job at the warehouse by my mom's place. Ask my uncle about his roofing guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stressed for real now.

S2.say: The office people are gonna come take our jobs now. They'll be flipping burgers.
S2.think: Laid-off graduates would be hired over him, so he'd be first cut.
S2.do: Does more delivery app shifts, applies at a nearby warehouse, and asks about roofing work through his uncle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's crazy rich people's stocks go up while everybody's broke. Somebody should just give people money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Physical work is safe, so I'd try to get into something like roofing or the warehouse. The fryer's okay too. But I'm up against a lot of people now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Actually go do the roofing thing. Or a forklift licence if it's cheap. Give my mom some money so she doesn't stress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I got a move.

S3.say: It's crazy rich people's stocks go up while everybody's broke. Just give people money.
S3.think: Physical work is safe, so he'd aim for roofing or warehouse work, though competition is tough.
S3.do: Starts roofing work or a cheap forklift licence and gives his mom money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's cooked. They took the tills, now the kitchen, the warehouse, the building sites. What's left for us?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every backup I said is gone. The fryer, the warehouse, the roofing. I didn't do great in school, so it's not like I'm gonna be an engineer. I'd be stuck at my mom's with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sign up for anything the government does, like training or that basic money thing. Try to get into something people still want a real person for. Maybe security. Maybe the gym, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lowkey scared. Like there's no lane for me.

S4.say: That's cooked. They took the tills, now the kitchen, the warehouse and the building sites.
S4.think: Every backup is gone, and without good grades he sees himself stuck at his mom's with nothing.
S4.do: Signs up for any government training or basic income and looks for jobs where people want a real person, like security.
S4.feel: Scared, with no lane for him.
